name: Net promoter score

seoDesc: Net promoter score: work out score 1 from the score 10 and the score 9. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: score 1 is what the Net promoter score calculator works out, and it gets there from the score 10, the score 9, the score 8 and the score 7. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Net promoter score calculator work?
sections.html:
The Net promoter score calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports score 1 in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the score 10, the score 9, the score 8 and the score 7.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Net promoter score calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Score 1=-score 0 − score 10 − score 2 − score 3 − score 4 − score 5 − score 6 − score 7 − score 8 − score 9 + total responses
Good responses (Promoter )=score 10 + score 9
Neutral responses (Passives )=score 7 + score 8
Bad responses (Detractors )=score 0 + score 1 + score 2 + score 3 + score 4 + score 5 + score 6
Bad responses (Detractors )=good responses (Promoter ) − 1 ÷ 100 × NPS × total responses
Neutral responses (Passives )=-bad responses (Detractors ) − good responses (Promoter ) + total responses

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Score 10 = 10 and Score 9 = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Good responses (Promoter ) = 20.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Good responses (Promoter ) = 20 should be roughly the size you expected from Score 10 = 10 and Score 9 = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Net promoter score calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the score 10, the score 9 and the score 8 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Net promoter score calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns score 1, derived from the score 10, the score 9 and the score 8. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Net promoter score calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the score 10, the score 9, the score 8 and the score 7, which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Good responses (Promoter ) = 20. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Net promoter score calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
